items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1965-09-13
items.q: Fats had a terrific influence on me too in those days.

ctx.x: Well, certainly your piano style goes beyond the ragtime realm. What have any other pianists of the swing era or the modern era influence your playing as it's constituted today?

I think that the first real impact that hit me, when I say impact, I was already going under the influence of the old timers like Jelly Roll and the ragtime pianists. And I had one pianist around here by the name of Buzzy Williams, who was very, very excellent, and he gave me a lot of encouragement and a lot of help. But getting back to the other pianists, I would say that the first one that really had a terrific impact on me was Earl Hines. I think that he did more to revolutionize my style of playing probably…
Did you take up, were you taken up much by Art Tatum's style?

items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1976-02-13
items.q: I used to pick up things from him, listening to him on records.

ctx.x: Right. He wasn't a flashy young man, but he had a great left hand.

Did you know him personally? Not personally, but I heard him a couple of times and he was very good. Very good. I knew some people that told me who he was, you know. But he never did play too much. I think he got sick or something, didn't he? Yeah. Because I never did hear too much of him. But he was good. And of course you had the other piano players that had the great impact like Fats Waller, you know, came along with his style of playing. Did he ever come down here? Yeah, but not, I think it was just him on a…
When I hear your piano, that's what I think of Earl Hines more than.
